1.pericope_label: Hear ye this word which I take up against you, even a lamentation, O house of Israel. The virgin of Israel is fallen; she shall no more rise
debates: Why Israel is called a virgin
How final the fall is
Who raises the lamentation
outliers: Calvin rejects as too refined the reading that makes the virgin a figure of spiritual espousal, since the prophets call Babylon and Egypt and Tyre virgins too, and takes it instead of a people living in delicacies
Clarke says the ten tribes are now totally lost among the nations, where Ellicott holds that Israel is not annihilated but obliterated as a nation and Calvin insists a tenth part would remain
themes: A word to be heard whether it is for us or against us
Judgment returning in each section louder than before
A people courted while high and slighted once fallen
A vessel broken to pieces on its own ground

3.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord God; The city that went out by a thousand shall leave an hundred. For thus saith the Lord unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live
debates: What the proportion of survivors means
Whether the call to seek God is open to all
What it is to live
outliers: Calvin inverts the military figure, noting that armies were decimated by losing a tenth while here only a tenth is saved, and holds that the word was designed to embitter the hypocrites as well as to comfort the few

Calvin distinguishes the design of public teaching, which calls all in common, from the secret purpose of God, which draws the elect and leaves the reprobate inexcusable, where Clarke and Gill present the offer simply as open on repentance
themes: A thousand marching out and a hundred coming back
A remnant hidden among a condemned multitude
A call that hardens some and gathers others
Repentance preached without faith effecting nothing

5.pericope_label: But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought
debates: What the play on the names of the shrines is
Why the call to seek God is repeated
Whether the threatened evil is still avoidable
outliers: Calvin sets aside the reading that makes the verse only a rebuke of hypocritical evasion, and holds that seeking God and seeking Bethel are wholly contrary things, superstition being condemnable in itself
Gill takes the repetition as a spur to a backward people, where Calvin makes it serve to leave hypocrites without excuse; Ellicott alone stresses that the curse is still conditional
themes: A house of God renamed a house of vanity
Men who take a circuitous road when called back
Worshippers asking why God will not indulge them a little
Fire rushing down on a kingdom

7.pericope_label: Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth, Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion
debates: Whether the doxology explains the rebuke before it
What the risings of the constellations mark
Who is strengthened against whom
outliers: Ellicott renders the closing line as desolation made to gleam upon the strong and to come upon the stronghold, where Gill, Clarke and Wesley all read it as the spoiled being strengthened against their conquerors

Wesley dates the rising of the seven stars to September and of Orion to November, where Ellicott makes the first a sign of spring and the second of the winter solstice; Calvin denies outright that the doxology explains the verse before it
themes: Justice turned as bitter as wormwood
A winner of his suit mourning over the costs
A god imagined small enough to be pacified cheaply
Judgments that used to pass by and now pass through

10.pericope_label: They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. Forasmuch therefore as your treading is upon the poor
debates: Who hates the reprover in the gate
Who the reprover is
What the burdens of wheat are
outliers: Clarke makes the wheat a fee taken for doing the poor man justice, where Ellicott makes it a voluntary gift of sifted corn offered to purchase the good will of the bench

Gill prefers the reading in which corrupt judges hate the prophets who reprove them, over the one in which a corrupt people hate faithful judges; Calvin agrees the judges are meant and extends the complaint to rulers of his own day
themes: A bench that cannot bear to be corrected
The poor made into the road their rulers walk on
A gift the giver was never obliged to make
A single word that may mean trampling or loading

12.pericope_label: For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right
debates: Who says that he knows their sins
Who the prudent are that keep silence
Why the silence is called prudent
outliers: Ellicott holds that the speaker who says I know is the prophet rather than Jehovah, against most commentators and against Calvin, who has God introduced as speaker precisely to give the threat authority

Gill excludes the prophets from the silent, since it was always their business to reprove, where Calvin allows that the teachers themselves did not oppose the torrent because it was not the time to resist violent men
themes: A judge whose splendour hides what a higher judge sees
A ransom paid to escape a harsh sentence
An office so heavy that some blame is expected
A prudent man laying his hand on his own mouth

14.pericope_label: Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the Lord, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken
debates: What the people meant by saying God was with them
Why hating evil is named before loving good
What the remnant of Joseph is
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin agree that the clause about what the people say reproves a merely outward confidence in descent and covenant, which Calvin says made circumcision a royal diadem to them
Clarke takes the remnant of Joseph for the posterity of the ten tribes at large, where Wesley limits it to what the invasions of enemies and the civil wars had left in Samaria and Israel
themes: A people seeking a curse while a blessing was offered
Men who reject God and still want him obliged to them
Satan gaining ground by degrees until right and wrong blur
An exhortation superfluous to one already willing

16.pericope_label: Therefore the Lord, the God of hosts, the Lord, saith thus; Wailing shall be in all streets; and they shall say in all the highways, Alas! alas!
debates: What the therefore looks back to
Why the husbandman is called to mourn
What passing through the midst means
outliers: Clarke explains the summons of the husbandman by a failure of the crops and a ground tilled in vain, where Ellicott and Wesley take it rather as proof that the disaster reached men who had no part in such ceremonies
Ellicott corrects the rendering of the two words for streets and would invert the last clause, so that the wailing is called to those skilled in lamentation rather than the reverse
themes: Mourning that will not stay indoors or keep decency
Hired mourners brought in where natural grief falls short
Wide squares by the gate and narrow alleys within
A visit longed for that comes as an enemy

18.pericope_label: Woe unto you that desire the day of the Lord! to what end is it for you? the day of the Lord is darkness, and not light
debates: Who desires the day of the Lord and why
What the lion and bear and serpent stand for
Whether the woe leaves any room for hope
outliers: Calvin rejects the exposition that makes the day of the Lord here the day of death and the desirers of it men bent on self-destruction, holding that the prophet is rousing hypocrites instead

Gill allows that the day desired may be the coming of Christ, wanted for temporal deliverance rather than salvation, where Clarke, Wesley and Henry all take it of the threatened judgment and Henry adds those who long for war in hope of rising on their country ruins
themes: A dark side to the pillar of fire
One evil escaped by calling in a worse ally
Hypocrites imitating faith as flowers without fruit
Darkness thick enough to be felt

21.pericope_label: I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies. Though ye offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept them
debates: Whose feasts are rejected
Why the sacrifices are hateful rather than merely useless
What the fat beasts of the peace-offerings are
outliers: Gill reports Kimchi referring the rejected feasts to the kingdom of Judah, which kept the feasts God commanded, and declines that reading in favour of the ten tribes imitating the worship at Jerusalem
Calvin distinguishes this prophet from the other prophets, who blame sacrifice for want of sincerity, holding that Amos blames it because the worshippers were apostates with a spurious temple
themes: Worshippers sitting as the people of God sit
A gift meant to buy leave to go on sinning
A blessing spoken loud enough to count as a curse
Veils spread before God to hide what he sees

23.pericope_label: Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream
debates: Why the music in particular is refused
Whether the last verse is exhortation or prophecy
How the verb about the stream should be rendered
outliers: Calvin sets out three expositions of the closing verse, an exhortation to purity of heart, a description of renewed life by its fruits, and a prophecy of the grace of Christ rolling on like a violent stream, and settles on the second

Clarke splits the two figures, making justice like fertilising showers and righteousness like a river that carries every abomination into the Dead Sea, where Ellicott merely corrects mighty stream to perennial stream
themes: Worship heaped up until no one can count it
Music that is only cutting and scraping without heart
An instrument named whose kind is now unknown
A river that sweeps the filth of a nation out to sea

25.pericope_label: Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel? But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images
debates: Whether sacrifices were offered at all in the wilderness
What was carried, and when
Why Damascus is named as the limit of the exile
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading that turns the verse into a threat of idols carried away into exile, holding that a vanquished nation does not carry its gods but has them carried off by the conquerors

Clarke denies that the question means no sacrifices at all were offered in the wilderness, listing those made at the covenant and the dedication, and takes it to ask whether they were offered in a way that pleased God
themes: Fathers and sons tied up in one bundle
A portable shrine carried along with the camp
A translator misled by one letter of a name
A fortress supposed to keep every enemy out
